<user>
Return the next passage of fiction.

I go to the house library and look on the open shelves for an introductory book about the Council. If I need help finding one, I ask whoever is working there.

item.text:
You leave the card game to its next hand and enter the library.

Lamp oil and old leather warm the air. Two levels of shelves rise around an iron spiral stair, their ends labeled in several scripts. At one reading table, Caelindra is reciting from the Vauldren travel journal while Seraphel listens.

“‘The inn’s eastern prospect is without equal,’” Caelindra reads. She turns the book to display an illustration of a blank stone wall. “He stayed there for nine days.”

Seraphel presses her knuckles to her mouth, containing another laugh.

The open shelves divide Council books into Founding, Accords, Procedure, Arbitration, and Commentaries. Several likely titles prove to be speeches, rebuttals, or multi-volume legal arguments. At the rear stands a locked glass cabinet marked *Restricted Covenant Histories—Chancellor’s Authorization Required*, but the introductory works are plainly meant to be elsewhere.

Beneath the spiral stair, an elderly human man works at a desk covered in notes. His scholar’s robe is frayed at both cuffs, and iron-grey hair falls forward whenever he bends over the page. He looks up as you approach, his gaze settling briefly on the Garvey signet.

“Garvey,” he says. “Professor Gareth Stone.”

“I’m looking for an introductory book about the Council.”

“There are introductions to its history and introductions to its procedure. For your purposes, you’ll need both.”

He rises and leads you to a low shelf you passed twice. The lettering on its brass label has nearly worn away.

Stone draws out a thick blue volume titled *Seven Seats in Session: Structure and Precedent*. Its binding is faded but sound. A much slimmer grey supplement follows.

“The blue book explains the Council as it was designed,” he says. “It predates the human vacancy, so its examples still assume seven voting seats. The supplement explains how procedure has changed since.”

From the reading table, Caelindra glances over. “The blue book also treats the Amber Court’s veto as ceremonial.”

“It was ceremonial when that edition was printed.”

“It isn’t now.”

Stone places the grey supplement atop the blue volume. “Hence the supplement.”

Caelindra accepts this with a slight tilt of one pointed ear and returns to the unfortunate traveler’s inn.

Stone lays both books on an empty table beneath a green-shaded lamp. “Begin with the first four chapters of the blue one. After that, alternate. Neither author reliably distinguishes law from custom, but reading them together makes the difference visible.”

The books are ordinary open-shelf copies, their borrowing cards largely blank. Stone returns to his notes, leaving you a clear table and a view of the library’s lower floor.
